events.summary: Gov. Greg Abbott signed a new map shifting five Democratic districts towards Republicans.
Gov. Mike Kehoe signed a new map; a referendum and court rulings later kept the 2022 map for November.
The General Assembly passed a new map (no governor's approval needed).
The Ohio Redistricting Commission unanimously approved a new map.
Voters approved Proposition 50, adopting the legislature's new map (AB 604) for 2026.
Judge Dianna Gibson chose the plaintiffs' map, adding a Democratic-leaning district.
A three-judge panel blocked the 2025 map; three days later the Supreme Court paused that ruling.
The Supreme Court ruled Texas could use the 2025 map in 2026.
A state judge blocked the redistricting amendment from the ballot.
The Virginia Supreme Court allowed the redistricting referendum on the 21 April ballot.
Voters approved the amendment allowing mid-decade redistricting.
The legislature approved a new map in a special session (House 83–23, Senate 21–17).
The Supreme Court ruled Louisiana's map an unconstitutional racial gerrymander (Louisiana v. Callais).
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed the new map into law.
The legislature passed, and Gov. Bill Lee signed, a map splitting the Memphis district.
The Virginia Supreme Court blocked the voter-approved plan; the old map stays.
The Supreme Court lifted the injunctions against the 2023 legislature map.
A lower court again blocked the 2023 map as a racial gerrymander.
Gov. Jeff Landry signed a new map shifting one Democratic district towards Republicans.
The Supreme Court lifted the lower-court order, so the 2023 map is used in 2026.
The Supreme Court stayed the Eighth Circuit order: the 2022 map is used in November.
